actions.reason: Three rounds of encode changes all produced identical outputs, but the best measured ratio was 0.9934 against the required 0.9900, so none were accepted. 1) The merge table now holds each row's bound dict.get, with a shared empty getter for ids that start no merge. This removes the None check and method lookup per scanned pair: encode_ir 0.9970. 2) BasicTokenizer.encode caches its sorted, validated replacement steps (same identity-plus-length staleness check as _get_merge_lookup): cumulative 0.9937. 3) In encode_ordinary, in-place += instead of the per-chunk extend call, plus a hoisted bound _encode_chunk: cumulative 0.9934, almost no change. train_ir drifted up to 1.0016, within limits. The per-chunk library work looks like only a few percent of the benchmark's instructions; most of the count appears to be fixed costs that can't be removed without changing behaviour. The only further idea needs a new merge-loop structure (incremental per-pair ranks, which needs a guard for non-monotonic merges). A similar rewrite measured worse earlier, and one evaluation was not enough to risk it.

journal.text:
I worked on encode in minbpe/regex.py and minbpe/basic.py. In regex.py the merge table now stores each row's bound dict.get, with one shared empty getter for ids that start no merge. That removes a None check and a method lookup per scanned pair. In basic.py, BasicTokenizer.encode now caches its sorted merges, and I trimmed the loop around it.

All three evaluations gave identical outputs and all three were rejected. Evaluation 1, regex.py only: encode_ir 400827492 to 399609358, ratio 0.9970. Evaluation 3, both files: ratio 0.9937, train_ir 1.0018. Evaluation 5: ratio 0.9934, train_ir 1.0016. The required ratio is 0.9900. I submitted no candidate.

Per-pair lookup overhead is not where encode spends most of its instructions. Shaving it gives well under one percent.

Next I want to profile encode_ir before editing. I will look at the pair scan and the list rebuilding on each merge. Avoiding repeated full rescans after each merge looks like the larger lever.
